title: Wardens Rising – Portfolio Page
description: Combat, AI, systems and economy design on an ARPG / tower defense hybrid at Big Moxi Games.

Page draft for the portfolio. Lines marked ASSET are things for you to find; brackets are facts to confirm. Everything else is ready to use.

ARPG / Tower Defense · Big Moxi Games · Unreleased (store page live)

Owned difficulty, economy and encounter balancing for an ARPG tower-defense game with 5 heroes, 7+ enemy archetypes and 40+ waves, from spreadsheet models to tuning in Unreal.

At a glance: 5 heroes · 7+ enemy archetypes · 40+ waves · 40+ progression pieces · 4 boss fights designed, 3 implemented

• What I owned: difficulty, economy and skill-tree balancing; every wave; boss design and behaviour; the tutorial.
  • Hardest problem: an endgame spike where enemies broke the core faster than players could react. Fixed with a targeting cap, counter-traps and an audio warning.

blocks.html:
Players defend a base with one of five heroes and placeable towers and traps, against waves of enemies coming through portals across several maps. It mixes action combat with tower-defense strategy, solo or in co-op. Between levels, players spend on items, perks, companions, skill-tree upgrades and new towers.

ASSET – 3–4 screenshots: a wide shot of a map mid-wave, the build mode with towers placed, the skill tree screen, and one boss.

• Five very different heroes, each needing to feel strong without one becoming the default pick.
  • Single-player and co-op had to work with the same waves, so difficulty had to scale with player count.
  • Engineering time was limited, so systems had to be data-driven: balance changes in tables, not code.
  • High enemy density stressed both readability and performance.

blocks.text: 2. Pacing: planning difficulty before the engine

blocks.html:
A campaign needs a clear sense of progression, and each level needs peaks of tension followed by short relief.

  • Gave every enemy a threat value, so a wave's difficulty could be calculated before it was built.
  • Mapped the difficulty curve across the campaign, with a Map × Invasion matrix to check the tension of every invasion on every map.
  • Built each level with rising and falling waves, then created all 40+ waves in the in-house wave tool inside Unreal: spawn portals, compositions and timers.

ASSET – Difficulty curve chart and the Map × Invasion matrix (both on the Wix page already).

Tower defense works when money is always a little short of what the next wave demands.

  • Balanced each wave's composition against the currency it pays out.
  • Set income per stage so upgrades never outran the defences players needed.
  • Built TTK and DPS models for heroes, towers and enemies, with charts that flag outliers, then moved the values into Unreal Data Assets.

Rather than flattening the heroes until they played alike, I kept them close in power and tuned the enemy archetypes against each hero's weaknesses. Each hero faces a different version of the same wave, so players change targets mid-fight and every hero keeps its identity.

  • Sorted the roster into clear combat roles (tanks, ranged, brawlers), each with its own stat template in Data Tables, so players read a threat at a glance and learn its counter.

ASSET – Hero × enemy matrix: a simple table of the 5 heroes against the 7 archetypes, marking where each hero is strong or weak. It shows this idea better than any paragraph. Draw it from memory if needed.

• Designed 40+ progression pieces (\[30+ items, 10 perks\], companions, skill-tree upgrades, tower unlocks), built on shared attribute modifiers in Data Tables so new content needed no custom code.
  • Modelled levelling speed and unlock timing with curves in Sheets, then exported them to Data Tables.
  • Tied key unlocks to specific stages (for example 1, 4 and 7), each introduced with a wave built to show off the new tower or trap.
  • Rebalanced less-picked items and perks; later playtests showed players using a wider range.
  • After playtests showed a late-game content drought, restructured the item and perk unlocks and moved tower milestones to line up with map transitions.

ASSET – Unlock timeline: the stages along a line, with each unlock marked. A screenshot of your unlock table also works.

I designed the tower-placement tutorial around situations players would actually meet, explained step by step, with room to try things rather than reading about mechanics in isolation. Onboarding ratings rose about 70% in playtests \[from X to Y\].

ASSET – Tutorial GIF: 10 seconds of the first tower placement step.

Bosses should test how players adapt, not just soak damage. I designed four; three were implemented.

  • Built multi-phase behaviour trees in Unreal; bosses switch between melee strings and ranged attacks depending on the player's distance.
  • Worked with level design on arenas, and with animation and VFX on telegraphs.

ASSET – Boss phase flow (on the Wix page) and a behaviour tree screenshot from Unreal, if allowed. A 10-second clip of a phase change is even better.

Iteration: the early bosses were designed without enough thought for the different heroes, so some heroes struggled badly. I changed attack ranges and damage and reshaped arenas with level design until each boss worked for all five. \[Which hero struggled most, and against which attack?\]

Problem: in dense waves, too many enemies targeted the player at once. The screen became noisy and damage arrived without warning.

Fix: a targeting cap with an aggro cooldown. Only a set number of enemies \[X\] can attack one player at a time; the rest go after the objectives.

Result: fights became readable again, and the overflow added a decision: protect yourself, or protect the base.

ASSET – Targeting cap before/after (on the Wix page).

blocks.text: Iteration case 1: the endgame core defense

blocks.html:
[embedded content: iteration case 1 · problem to result\]

Problem: in endgame levels, players defend a core protected by power nodes. Telemetry showed that certain high-threat archetypes stripped the core's shields faster than players could react, creating an unfair difficulty spike.

Cause: those enemies arrived in numbers and all went straight for the nodes, with no warning.

Options considered: \[list what you actually discussed, for example lowering their damage, adding more defences, or slowing their spawn, and why each was rejected\].

Fix:

  1. Reduced their numbers and added a shared targeting cap for node-attacking enemies.
  2. Added traps and items that pull enemy focus away from the nodes.
  3. Added a voice line when node threats spawn, so players can reposition in time.

Result: the next playtests showed the spike flattened and the level back to a steady defensive rhythm. \[Add a number: failure rate or core-loss rate before and after.\]

ASSET – The case-study image from the Wix page, plus a death heatmap of that level before the fix, if you can get one.

I treated playtesting as a loop: focused test phases on specific features, new biomes and hero balance; surveys I wrote and ran; reports from external playtest agencies turned into design tasks.

Cross-checking these let me act on what players did, not just what they said. Across test rounds, survey scores rose about 60% \[from X to Y on what scale\].

ASSET – A telemetry heatmap, blurred if needed, and one survey chart showing scores across rounds. These two images prove the data-driven claims on this page.

• Balance through enemies, not heroes. Harder to tune, since every archetype interacts with five heroes, but it kept each hero distinct.
  • Targeting cap over lower enemy counts. Fewer enemies would have fixed readability but killed the feeling of a horde; the cap kept density and added a decision.
  • Data tables over custom code. Slower to set up, but it let design rebalance without waiting for engineering.

• 40+ waves, 3 bosses and 40+ progression pieces built and tuned in engine.
  • Survey scores up about 60% and onboarding ratings up about 70% across playtest rounds.
  • The game reached a public store page but has not launched; \[say what you can about its status\].

What worked: planning difficulty in spreadsheets before building, and triangulating telemetry with surveys.

What I'd do differently: \[pick what's true, for example: design bosses against all five heroes from the start; set measurable difficulty targets before the first test round\].

What I learned: with several heroes, balancing through the enemies keeps each hero's identity; telemetry shows where players struggle, surveys explain why.
